rv.q: Several key characters, including the mighty Titans and Hercules’s dim but loyal equine friend Pegasus, have been excised. Panic and Pain, the demonic shapeshifters on team Hades, are now a couple of deadbeat blokes called Bob and Charles. The irritable satyr Philoctetes is now a world weary, very human waiter.
Hercules, though, is one unit of generic Disney stage entertainment.
There’s not much more to it, but as far as it goes, it’s amiable fun.

What emerges is a snappily staged pantomime, complete with villain, comic sidekicks, love interest, slash-and-bash fight scenes and even a “he’s behind you” moment of sorts, as Hercules sprints across the stage with a monster in hot pursuit.
So there is a stolidity to the story, as if an ancient tablet of stone has taken the place of a flesh and blood heart.

But in the ranks of Disney stage adaptations it feels closer to the mediocre Frozen (which lasted just three years at this theatre from 2021-4) than the all-conquering The Lion King (25 years in the similarly-sized Lyceum, and still going strong).
Still, it’s hard to work up much enthusiasm about Casey Nicholaw’s musclebound production at Theatre Royal Drury Lane.
Nicholaw’s staging is remorselessly cheery: not so much humorous as perpetually grinning; not so much moving on – choreography is more vigorous than expressive – as jumping on the spot.
Unfortunately, there’s none of the same imaginative energy in this stodgy new stage version, which hits the expected beats without capturing the lovable zaniness that makes Hercules a fan fave.
At best, this is an enjoyable summer romp that’s very far from pretentious.
It’s not a disaster, but it is oddly dull.
I would recommend that you go quite some distance to avoid this.
Casey Nicholaw's production packs in big tunes, gorgeous costumes, and plenty of groan-worthy laughs.
It is a show scaled to the venue, a show to be treated as fun—don’t take it seriously!
It’s an enjoyable theatrical production, but struggles to find the sweet spot between being a silly show for kids and a more adult musical about finding your place in the world.
That may induce a sigh from me, but I suspect Joe Tex and family felt they got their money’s worth.
It isn’t a bad night out, but it’s like a fizzy drink, lively on the tongue but ultimately unsatisfying.
Between them, they lift a fragile show that still has a great distance to go on the way to success.
But having a super-saturated production insist upon you having a good time all the time proves less entertaining, more enervating.
This lustre-dusted show-stopper of a musical is everything you could want.
Hercules is a heroic hit, complete with tunics, thunderbolts, and toe-tapping tunes.
It's not the deepest of Disney stories, but director and choreographer Casey Nicholaw invests it with terrific action-packed energy and tongue in cheek humour.
The good is unevenly distributed but still present.
The stage adaptation of Hercules is a strange one - it has its strengths, but they prove inconsistent, and the wheels do fall off slightly along the way.
It may put "the glad in Gladiator", but not in my heart.
‘Hercules’ is funny and fierce plus ticks all the boxes if you’re looking for a family-friendly mood-lifter.
The two hour show is packed with one-liners that are as strong as Hercules’ fists, and just as punchy too.
But while it's far from a zero, it's not quite a hero either, and the gospel truth is that the Hercules musical is a mixed bag.

cn.t: Disney's Hercules delivers slick, family-friendly spectacle with powerhouse Muses and catchy Menken tunes, but critics find it mechanical and charm-free compared to stronger Disney adaptations, calling it more polished panto than theatrical magic.
